sourceBindings.text: Carrots are wanted in heavy clay used by machinery; roots are forked and the site stays wet.
Measure compaction depth, wetness/drainage, chemistry and growing-season constraints rather than assuming clay texture is the sole cause.
Management path: redirect traffic, consider tested organic input and a drained, designed raised growing zone; retain the source's dimensions only as provisional study examples.
Alternative path: assess a locally suitable drained-row leafy crop or bean, or managed rice/taro only with a suitable climate and water system; do not call beans flood-tolerant.
Both paths have a reason and a stop condition; success and cost require local verification.

sourceBindings.text: Three stages, not a miracle cure
A low-OM former machinery path is to be considered for vegetables over 3–6 months.
Baseline root and soil tests, traffic stop and moisture/drainage diagnosis.
Select and document amendments, cover/bed and if justified a controlled physical action under suitable conditions.
Retest, observe roots and water, compare with baseline and only then trial a crop or revise the timetable.
Compost can aid organic matter and supply variable nutrients; targeted mineral fertilizer may address nutrient deficiency but not a compacted layer.

sourceBindings.text: Choose a land use that holds soil
The bank describes a very shallow, rocky hillside with no demonstrated deep cultivation layer.
Compare the bank's carrots/potatoes, corn, rice paddy and pasture-grass/herb alternatives by rooting zone and disturbance.
Select a locally adapted, established vegetative cover as the initial lower-erosion option; verify species, water and grazing management.
Retain residue and minimize disturbance where feasible, but plan runoff control and establishment; no-till alone is not a complete engineering design.
Conditional pasture/ground cover is stronger than a deep-rooted or flooded annual crop for this described shallow slope.
